hero.title: Arrays
intro.0: Sooner or later one value is not enough - you have a row of names, a run of scores, a line of readings. An array holds many values in a fixed, ordered row, and lets you reach any one by its position. You write each move and run it.
task.1.title: Read by position
task.1.context:
An **array** is a fixed-size, ordered row of values - like numbered lockers, each holding one item. You reach an item by its **position**, counting from `0`: the first item is `names[0]`, the second is `names[1]`.

Write a `Kennel` whose `First(string[] names)` hands back the name in the first locker.
task.1.goal.0: Give `Kennel` a `string First(string[] names)` that returns the item at position `0`.
task.1.goal.1: `Main` calls `First` with `"Rex"`, `"Milo"`, `"Bella"`, so the output is `Rex`.
task.2.title: How many items
task.2.context:
Every array knows its own size - how many lockers it has. The idea is the same in any language: ask the sequence how many items it holds. In C# you read it with `.Length`.

Write a `Tally` whose `Count(int[] xs)` returns how many numbers are in the array.
task.2.goal.0: Give `Tally` an `int Count(int[] xs)` that returns `xs.Length`.
task.2.goal.1: `Main` calls `Count` with five numbers, so the output is `5`.
task.3.title: Add them up
task.3.context:
To use every item, you **walk** the array from start to end. A `foreach` loop hands you each item in turn, so you can add them up as you go - a running total that grows one item at a time.

Write a `Meter` whose `Sum(int[] xs)` walks the array and returns the total.
task.3.goal.0: Give `Meter` an `int Sum(int[] xs)` that walks `xs` with a `foreach` loop and adds each item.
task.3.goal.1: `Main` calls `Sum` with `2`, `3`, `5`, so the output is `10`.
task.4.title: Count the big ones
task.4.context:
Walking an array is not only for adding - you can **decide** something about each item as you pass it. Test each one, and count the ones that pass.

Write a `Sieve` whose `HowManyBig(int[] xs)` walks the array and returns how many items are greater than `10`.
task.4.goal.0: Give `Sieve` an `int HowManyBig(int[] xs)` that walks `xs` and counts the items greater than `10`.
task.4.goal.1: `Main` calls `HowManyBig` with `3`, `20`, `7`, `50`, so the output is `2`.
task.5.title: Split text into pieces
task.5.concept: Text into an array with Split
task.5.context:
Text often hides a sequence inside it - `"cat,dog,fish"` is really three items joined by commas. `Split` cuts the text at each separator and hands back a `string[]` you can measure and walk, just like any array you build by hand.

Write a `Line` whose `Pieces(string csv)` returns how many comma-separated items the text holds.
task.5.goal.0: Give `Line` an `int Pieces(string csv)` that splits `csv` on `','` and returns the count of pieces.
task.6.title: What you learned
task.6.context: Five everyday moves on an array - the ordered row of values you reach for whenever you have more than one of something.
task.6.summaryIntro: An array holds many values in a fixed, ordered row. You reached into it, measured it, walked it and built one from text:
task.6.summaryItems.0.title: Read by position -
task.6.summaryItems.0.text: `names[0]` reaches the item in the first locker; positions count from `0`.
task.6.summaryItems.1.title: How many items -
task.6.summaryItems.1.text: `xs.Length` asks the array how many values it holds.
task.6.summaryItems.2.title: Add them up -
task.6.summaryItems.2.text: a `foreach` loop hands you each item in turn, so you can total them as you walk.
task.6.summaryItems.3.title: Walk and decide -
task.6.summaryItems.3.text: test each item as you pass it and count the ones that pass.
task.6.summaryItems.4.title: Split text into pieces -
task.6.summaryItems.4.text: `csv.Split(',')` turns text into a `string[]` you can measure and walk like any other array.
task.6.summaryClose: An array's size is fixed once you make it. When you need a row that grows or shrinks, you will reach for a list next - but every move you just learned carries straight over.
